findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Service savings strategy abandoned; discovered significant savings could not be achieved without adversely affecting service delivery
findings.detail: The 2025/26 MTFS required recurring service reductions of £1.78m, increasing to £3.781m by 2027/28. A discovery phase concluded that 'significant savings or lower-priority services could not be readily identified without adversely affecting service delivery.' The council then ceased this savings strategy, switched to relying on reserves, and moved planned efficiencies to the North Hampshire Unitary Authority.
findings.matters: The council has abandoned sustainable cost-cutting and is instead treating short-term reserve depletion as its financial strategy, suggesting structural problems with its cost base.
findings.figures: 2025/26 required service reductions: £1.78m. Planned 2027/28 reduction: £3.781m (no longer pursued).
findings.quote: it ceased the service prioritisation savings strategy, maintained a no net budget growth approach other than unavoidable pressures, and planned to use reserves where necessary.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Council reserves will be drawn down to fund structural deficits, with estimated £2.253m available at Vesting Day before risks
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £2.362m deficit in 2025/26 (now better at £2.362m from reserves). Going forward, it plans deficits of £442k in 2026/27 and £2.694m annually from 2027/28, to be met from reserves. Estimated available reserves at Vesting Day: £2.253m, but this is before accounting for the risks outlined (property income, receipts delays, Serco, LGR).
findings.matters: The council is structurally deficit and treating reserves as a funding source, not a contingency, with limited buffer remaining against the material risks identified.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn deficit: £2.362m. Reserves at 31 March 2026: £6.914m. Estimated at Vesting Day: £2.253m (before risks).
findings.quote: the estimated revenue reserves available to fund the forecast deficit at Vesting Day have increased from £1.828 million to £2.253 million before consideration of the risks outlined below.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs expected to be significant but not yet budgeted in the MTFS
findings.detail: LGR cost apportionment methodology across Hampshire is still being assessed. Costs are expected to be significant and will place 'additional demands on available reserves.' While some may be funded through Flexible Use of Capital Receipts, 'a substantial proportion is expected to fall directly on the revenue budget.' No additional provision has been included in this MTFS update beyond existing assumptions.
findings.matters: A material unfunded cost burden is likely to emerge after this MTFS was set, putting further pressure on reserves and cashflow.
findings.figures: None quantified in the paper; costs still being assessed.
findings.quote: These costs are expected to be significant and will place additional demands on available reserves. While some expenditure may qualify for funding through the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Direction, a substantial proportion is expected to fall directly on the revenue budget. No additional provision has been included within this MTFS update beyond existing assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Serco contract renegotiation concluding September 2026 with risk of cost pressures beyond current £1.095m budget
findings.detail: Contract negotiations conclude in September 2026. The council has provisioned £500k plus a further £595k in the current forecast. Under either the existing arrangement or a move to Twin Stream model, the council must procure and fund vehicles and equipment. The paper acknowledges 'risk of additional cost pressures arising beyond the current budget assumptions.'
findings.matters: A major service contract is being renegotiated with material uncertain costs that could exceed budget in either outcome scenario.
findings.figures: February 2026 provision: £500k. Additional assumed in current review: £595k. Total: £1.095m.
findings.quote: The Council will be able to either continue the existing contract arrangements or move to a Twin Stream service model. Under either option, the Council will be responsible for procuring and funding vehicles and equipment. There remains a risk of additional cost pressures arising beyond the current budget assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Audit of 2025/26 outturn not yet completed; adjustments could materially impact reported position and forecasts
findings.detail: The 2025/26 position reported in this paper is provisional. The council explicitly notes it 'has not yet achieved an unqualified audited financial position' and that audit adjustments could impact the reported outturn and forward financial forecasts. Any such impacts will be reflected in subsequent monitoring reports.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on the financial position stated here—the final audited outturn and any audit qualifications could reveal material issues not currently disclosed.
findings.figures: Reported 2025/26 outturn deficit: £2.362m (provisional, unaudited).
findings.quote: Given that the Council has not yet achieved an unqualified audited financial position, there remains a risk that adjustments arising from the completion of the audit process could impact the Council's reported financial position and future financial forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Four major capital disposals all delayed 9-15 months, forcing extended external borrowing
findings.detail: Devereux House (15 months late), Hawley Lane (12+ months), Meads Block 3 (9+ months), and Union Yard (9 months, with £500k value reduction). The council explicitly states these delays 'increase the level and duration of external borrowing required to maintain liquidity.' Borrowing rates are also higher than the 4.5% assumption in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Delayed asset sales force extended external borrowing at higher rates than budgeted, materially worsening cashflow and increasing interest costs.
findings.figures: Union Yard: budgeted £15m May-25, forecast £14.5m July-26 (£500k reduction, 9-month delay). Devereux House: 15-month delay. Hawley Lane: 12+ months. Meads Block 3: 9+ months.
findings.quote: Delays in achieving planned capital receipts continue to impact the Council's treasury position by increasing the level and duration of external borrowing required to maintain liquidity. Uncertainty over the timing of asset disposals reduces flexibility in cashflow management and limits opportunities to reduce borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn, 2026-27 Q1 forecast and MTFS update - Report No. FIN2613
findings.headline: Commercial property income faces material decline and lease-break risk over the MTFS period
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a comprehensive review of rental income forecasts and lease expiries. Income declines from £9.8m in 2026/27 to £6.5m by 2029/30. Income at risk outside lease breaks grows from £137k to £3.2m over the period. Service costs and business rates at Ashbourne House are expected to increase significantly. The paper explicitly warns this could have 'material adverse impact on the revenue budget and the Council's financial resilience.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a major income stream is contracting and vulnerable to further deterioration through tenant defaults or lease exits.
findings.figures: Income up to lease break/exit: £9.8m (26/27) declining to £6.5m (29/30). Income at risk outside lease: £136,634 (26/27) to £3,223,907 (29/30).
findings.quote: Any reduction in occupancy levels or rental income could have a material adverse impact on the revenue budget and the Council's financial resilience leading up to Vesting Day.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Commercial property income of £7.9m–£8.3m covers 47–57% of financing costs but exposed to property market risk
findings.detail: The council holds commercial property investments acquired 2016–2021 generating net annual income of £7.9m (2024/25 actual), £8.1m (2025/26 forecast), £8.3m (2026/27 estimate). This income covers a material proportion of financing costs: 57.1% of net core revenue stream in 2024/25, declining to 47.7% by 2026/27. Property market downturns, tenant defaults, or lease expirations could materially impair this income and worsen the council's financial position.
findings.matters: Commercial income substitutes for other revenue sources. Unlike grants or tax income, it faces market and tenant covenant risk. A lender would need confidence this income is resilient to property market stress.
findings.quote: Between 2016 and 2021 in the context of central government financial support for local public services declining, the Council undertook some investment in commercial properties purely or mainly for financial gain.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Strategic cessation of new capital borrowing; capital programme contracted from £14.7m to £3.6m over two years
findings.detail: Debt-financed capital spending has fallen from £8.4m (2024/25) to £4.3m (2025/26) to £0 planned for 2026/27 onwards. The overall capital programme has contracted correspondingly from £14.7m (2024/25) to £3.6m (2026/27), £2.7m (2027/28), £2.5m (2028/29). Future capital will be financed entirely from government grants and capital receipts. This represents a sustained tightening of capital investment capacity.
findings.matters: A council with no capacity for new capital borrowing faces constraints on asset investment and service development. Sustained under-investment in assets can lead to deterioration and reduced service capacity.
findings.quote: In 202 6/27, the Council is planning capital expenditure of £ 3.6m as summarised below

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Farnborough leisure centre capital project contingent on securing guaranteed operator income and achieving annual cost-neutrality
findings.detail: The council has included a leisure centre development at Farnborough in its capital strategy but explicitly conditions it on 'securing guaranteed operator income sufficient to fund the required borrowing to bridge the gap between the cost of build and the remaining Levelling Up Funding'. The project must also be 'at least cost neutral every year'. This is a conditional commitment, not a confirmed project.
findings.matters: A capital scheme dependent on third-party operator guarantees is higher-risk than council-funded investment. If guarantees are not secured, the project does not proceed, affecting both capital investment and debt reduction plans.
findings.figures: Farnborough leisure centre; contingent on operator income guarantee; must be cost-neutral annually; leverages Levelling Up Funding
findings.quote: The Council's ambition to build a leisure centre at Farnborough is dependent upon securing guaranteed operator income sufficient to fund the required borrowing to bridge the gap between the cost of build and the remaining Levelling Up Funding allocated by government, the overall revenue impact on the Council must be at least cost neutral every year.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: £23.6m capital receipts forecast for 2026/27 to finance capital programme; timing and proceeds explicitly flagged as uncertain
findings.detail: The council plans to receive £23.6m capital receipts in 2026/27 (up from £4.8m in 2025/26) to finance capital expenditure and debt reduction, with zero new borrowing. The strategy explicitly flags 'uncertainties around the timing of asset sales and the amount that assets can be sold for', and acknowledges these 'amounts may be different or be received in different years'. Shortfalls would delay both capital investment and debt reduction.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are essential to the council's debt reduction plan and capital programme. If sales are delayed or underprice, both investment and debt management timescales will slip.
findings.figures: £4.8m capital receipts (2025/26 forecast), £23.6m (2026/27 estimate); 2026/27 capital financing: £1.5m grants, £2.1m receipts, £0 borrowing
findings.quote: There is the possibility that these amounts may be different or be received in different years.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 - Annual Capital Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Borrowing of £159m explicitly declared unsustainable; £32.9m asset sales over four years planned to remedy, but timing and proceeds uncertain
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, the council holds £159m borrowing at 4.7% weighted average rate. The strategy explicitly states current debt is not sustainable and plans £32.9m of asset sales (and FIL loan repayment) over four years to reduce it. However, the council acknowledges 'uncertainties around the timing of asset sales and the amount that assets can be sold for', creating material execution risk on the debt reduction trajectory.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a credible path to sustainable debt. This council recognises the problem and has a plan, but depends on executing substantial asset sales at uncertain prices and timescales.
findings.figures: £159.0m borrowing at 31 December 2025; £32.9m asset sales/repayment planned over four years; financing costs 50.6% of net core revenue (2024/25)
findings.quote: The current high levels of borrowing are not considered to be affordable on a long term, sustainable basis. For this reason, asset sales (and FIL loan repayment) of £32.9m over the next four years are expected to reduce borrowing to a more affordable level.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: External auditor Ernst Young raises sustained concerns about the council's progress on achieving financial sustainability and resolving its deficit; the auditor is considering whether to issue a public interest report.
findings.detail: For the second consecutive year, Ernst Young's audit report raises concerns about the council's financial sustainability. The auditor has not ruled out issuing a public interest report—an extraordinary step that overrides normal democratic controls and escalates the council's financial situation to national scrutiny. The auditor has already held a member-only briefing to flag these concerns.
findings.matters: Independent auditor concern validates the severity of the council's financial position. A potential public interest report would be a major red flag for any lender and would trigger external intervention by government or regulator.
findings.figures: Concerns raised for second consecutive year (2023/24 and 2024/25 audit reports)
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Annual Audit report was presented to the Audit and Governance committee on 28th January 2026, and being consistent with the previous year's report, raises concerns regarding the council's progress on achieving financial sustainability and resolving its deficit. EY have a duty to consider if it is appropriate to raise a public interest report, with the very grave effect of overriding the democratic control of the council.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council's Financial Statements have disclaimed audit opinions back to 2020/21, meaning the opening reserve balances are not independently verified; full audit assurance won't be achieved until February 2029.
findings.detail: The council's external auditor (Ernst Young) has not been able to sign off on the council's accounts for several years due to audit delays. This means there is no independent verification that the reserves the council claims to hold actually exist or are adequate. The council will not have a clean audit opinion until February 2029—well into the post-merger period.
findings.matters: Unaudited reserves are unverified. A council's ability to balance its budget depends on having sufficient reserves to draw upon, but if those reserves have never been independently verified, the true financial position is unknown. There is risk that reserves are lower than stated.
findings.figures: Disclaimed audit opinions back to 2020/21; full audit assurance not expected until February 2029
findings.quote: Financial Statements disclaimed audit backlog to 2020/21 carries risk around impact on available reserves. Full audit assurance will not be achieved until the 2026/27 financial statements audit is completed by audit deadline of February 2029.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council must borrow £149m by end of 2026/27 and refinance £74m of maturing debt; interest rate sensitivity is acute—a 0.5% rate rise adds £300k annually to borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Rushmoor has substantial borrowing needs to fund capital programmes. The MTFS assumes interest rates will settle at 4.5%, but treasury officers are actively managing the timing of new borrowing to lock in rates. However, the council's budget cannot absorb unexpected rate movements. The risk register quantifies this: even a modest 0.5% increase costs £300k/year—a material portion of reserves given current constraints.
findings.matters: A council's ability to manage borrowing costs determines whether reserves last long enough to reach the merger date. Interest rate risk is real and uninsurable; rate movements are outside the council's control but directly impact budget sufficiency.
findings.figures: £149m borrowing requirement by end 2026/27; £74m debt maturing in 2026/27; assumed interest rate 4.5%; 0.5% rate rise = £300k/year additional cost
findings.quote: The council as part of its previous strategy for funding prior year capital programmes will have a need to borrow £149m by the end of 2026/27 before the application of capital receipts

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The £5m-per-annum waste collection contract with Serco has not been concluded; negotiations remain open on 'significant cost and capital commitment risks'.
findings.detail: The contract renewal is unsettled despite the contract value being approximately £5m annually. The council identifies 'significant cost and capital commitment risks' that 'must be engaged with and understood as early as possible'. No clear resolution date is given, and the risk is flagged as requiring ongoing engagement.
findings.matters: Waste collection is a core statutory service. An unresolved contract with a value equivalent to significant budget pressure means the council faces potential cost escalation or service disruption mid-financial-year if negotiation breaks down.
findings.figures: ~£5m annual contract value; specific cost and capital risks identified but not quantified
findings.quote: The Waste collection contract with Serco (circa £5m) negotiations to extend the contract have not been concluded. There are some significant cost and capital commitment risks associated with this contract that must be engaged with and understood as early as possible to enable any potential mitigation to be effective.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The Farnborough Leisure Centre project will generate £806k of net annual revenue cost between 2026 and 2028, before improving after 2028—scope and cost still being finalised.
findings.detail: The council is building a new leisure centre with uncertain final cost. The 2026/27 budget includes an estimated £806k annual revenue drain (including additional borrowing interest and MRP) for the first three years, but 'work on scoping the cost of a leisure centre on the Civic Quarter site is still underway' and a proposal will not reach Cabinet until March 2026. Budget and treasury strategies will need adjustment once Cabinet decides to proceed.
findings.matters: A major capital project with not-yet-finalised scope and cost adds revenue pressure to an already-stressed budget. If final costs exceed estimates, the council will have to find additional savings or borrowing during a period when it has little flexibility.
findings.figures: £806k net annual revenue expenditure impact 2026–2028 (including borrowing interest and MRP); project scope still being scoped
findings.quote: the council is proposing to progress the Farnborough Leisure Centre with a net revenue expenditure impact in the short-term 2026-2028 of £806k, including additional borrowing interest and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP).

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council holds an unsecured £6.5m loan to Farnborough International Limited (FIL) repayable in tranches over the next three years; FIL's financial stability is flagged as a material risk.
findings.detail: The council has lent £6.482m to a private company with no apparent security or right to recover if the company fails. The council reviews FIL's trading and cashflow quarterly, but the risk is explicitly identified in the risk register as requiring 'continue engagement'—indicating ongoing concern about repayment.
findings.matters: An unsecured loan to a potentially unstable company concentrates credit risk; if FIL defaults, the council loses £6.5m from already-depleted reserves, forcing either further asset sales or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £6.482m unsecured loan due in tranches over three years
findings.quote: There is an unsecured loan to Farnborough International Limited (FIL) of £6.482m due for repayment in tranches in the next three years.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: If the council's planned merger into a new unitary authority is delayed beyond April 2028, the 2028/29 budget position will require a Section 114 notice—effectively ceasing all non-essential spending.
findings.detail: The council's financial projections assume the merger completes on schedule. The S151 officer warns that if the merger is delayed, the 2028/29 projection 'will, based upon these projections, require a S114(3)'. A Section 114 notice is a severe governance intervention triggered when a council cannot meet its liabilities and halts discretionary expenditure immediately.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is an emergency measure that signals insolvency risk and material uncertainty over a council's ability to continue operations. For a lender, it represents the worst-case financial outcome short of the council entering administration.
findings.figures: 2028/29 financial projection triggers S114 risk if Vesting Day (1 April 2028) is delayed
findings.quote: the MTFS and related risks will be kept under constant review during the year and will be brought to the new council's attention at the earliest opportunity to draw attention to the 2028/29 financial projection, which otherwise will, based upon these projections, require a S114(3) if the council were delayed or not to be absorbed into a new council on 1st April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: The council's entire savings plan depends on achieving capital receipts from asset sales in specific timescales; any slippage forces immediate emergency expenditure cuts.
findings.detail: The MTFS budget is built on the assumption that planned asset disposals will be completed and credited on time. If these sales slip or fetch lower values, the council has no other mitigation—it must cut spending in-year to balance the budget. The council explicitly warns that 'further slippage in the timing and value of capital receipts during 2026/27' will force compensatory cuts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's budget plan is resilient. When a council cannot balance its books without selling assets on a fixed timeline, that plan is fragile and vulnerable to market conditions or legal delays.
findings.figures: Planned asset receipts are material to reducing borrowing costs and MRP; no specific forward figure given but identified as 'a material element'
findings.quote: Should there be any further slippage in the timing and value of capital receipts during 2026/27, the council will have to compensate by an appropriate level of in year expenditure reductions.

findings.paper_title: Annex 4 - General Fund Budget 2627 and MTFS 202627 to 202930
findings.headline: Ongoing structural deficit will continue beyond the council's planned merger date, with £11.94m total shortfall over four years requiring reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The council faces a recurrent annual deficit that continues past the April 2028 Vesting Day when it merges into a new unitary. Even after accounting for planned asset sales reducing the shortfall to £3.962m, the council will draw down £3.05m of reserves between 2026-2028. This leaves an uncertain financial position for the new authority.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves indicate structural spending exceeds revenue, and the deficit persists beyond the restructuring—meaning the new council inherits an unsustainable position unless urgent action is taken.
findings.figures: £11.94m gross deficit 2026/27–2029/30; £3.962m shortfall after asset sales; £3.05m reserve drawdown 2026–2028; £3.384m useable reserves projected at Vesting Day
findings.quote: The proposed 2026/27 MTFS therefore has an ongoing recurrent annual deficit going beyond Vesting Day.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Short-term debt maturity remains elevated at 53% due within 12 months, creating near-term refinancing risk
findings.detail: Although the council has reduced the proportion of loans maturing within 12 months from 91% to 53%, this remains a significant refinancing risk. Half of the £159.0m borrowing portfolio matures within the next 12 months and will need to be refinanced, potentially in a higher interest rate environment or tighter credit conditions.
findings.matters: High short-term maturity concentration creates refinancing risk. If market access tightens or rates rise materially, the council faces higher costs on rollover. The near-term refinancing cliff is a key credit risk metric.
findings.figures: 53% of loans due within 12 months (down from 91% previous year); approximately £80m of £159.0m borrowing due within 12 months
findings.quote: The Council has taken recent steps to reduce the proportion of loans maturing in under 12 months: this is now 53% of loans in contrast to the previous year when this was 91% of loans.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council contingent on imminent local government reorganisation in its treasury strategy; states it has only two years remaining
findings.detail: Paragraph 4.6 of the borrowing strategy states: 'the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account.' This appears to reference a planned local government reorganisation or merger affecting Rushmoor. This creates uncertainty over the appropriateness of treasury forecasts beyond 2027-28 and affects the council's ability to lock in long-term borrowing arrangements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a structural change to the council (merger, reorganisation) is imminent and how this affects the council's financial obligations and treasury management autonomy. This is material to credit assessment and loan agreements.
findings.figures: Two-year timeframe before restructuring
findings.quote: However, the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio shows cumulative losses and council is heavily dependent on investment income to balance budget
findings.detail: The council holds £148.2m in commercial property investments with a cumulative unrealised loss of £11.2m (purchase cost £159.4m vs. value in accounts £148.2m). Significant sector losses include retail (£14.8m) and offices (£7.0m). More significantly, the council relies on investment income to fund 29.5% of gross service expenditure in 2026-27 (forecast investment income £10.1m against gross service expenditure £34.2m). The strategy states that if properties fall below purchase cost at year-end, an updated strategy will be presented to council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's revenue dependency on asset values and market returns. A downturn in property values or rental income would create both balance sheet losses and revenue budget shortfalls. This represents significant concentration risk.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio value £148.2m (purchase cost £159.4m, loss £11.2m); investment income £10.1m forecast 2026-27; gross service expenditure £34.2m; investment income represents 29.5% of service expenditure
findings.quote: The Council has become increasingly dependent on surplus generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Strategic shift to internal borrowing reduces external debt but depletes cash reserves significantly
findings.detail: The council is reducing reliance on external borrowing in favour of internal borrowing (using cash reserves). External borrowing is forecast to fall sharply from £166.0m (2024-25 actual) to £75.0m (2026-27) to £25.0m (2028-29). Simultaneously, internal borrowing is forecast to increase from £7.9m to £110.5m over the same period. This strategy depletes the council's available working capital significantly and increases vulnerability to cash flow disruptions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council is managing its liquidity and whether internal borrowing (depleting reserves) is sustainable. High internal borrowing reduces financial flexibility and cash buffers.
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 - Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council planning £70m additional borrowing by 2028-29 despite falling Capital Financing Requirement
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to decrease from £174.2m to £135.5m over the forecast period, yet the council expects to need £70.0m of additional borrowing by 2028-29. This is driven by a significant refinancing requirement: £159.0m of loans were held as at 31 December 2025, with around half maturing within 12 months and the remainder within 5 years. The underlying need to refinance maturing debt outweighs the declining CFR.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt maturity profile and refinancing needs. Large refinancing requirements over the next 5 years create refinancing risk, particularly in a rising interest rate environment or credit stress.
findings.figures: £159.0m borrowing at 31 Dec 2025; £70.0m additional borrowing needed by 2028-29; around half of current debt due within 12 months; remaining loans due within 5 years
findings.quote: a significant proportion of the currently held loans are due to mature over the next five years' and will need to be replaced, meaning the Council can expect to have an ongoing borrowing need in future even though the CFR is falling. Over the forecast period above it is expected that £70.0m of additional borrowing will be needed by 2028-29.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Journal authorisation control failure: large journal adjustment above £20,000 was not properly reviewed or approved.
findings.detail: During testing of journal authorisation controls, EY found that a journal entry above £20,000 relating to a PPE impairment was not properly reviewed and authorised by the Deputy Section 151 Officer as required by management policy. While EY determined the underlying adjustment was supportable, the control failure represents a material gap in financial review procedures.
findings.matters: Weak journal authorisation controls are a primary fraud risk and allow errors or irregularities to be processed without oversight. This is a fundamental control that underpins financial reporting accuracy.
findings.figures: Journal above £20,000 threshold without proper evidence of review
findings.quote: During journal testing, we were unable to obtained evidence that a journal above £20,000 was approved by Deputy S151 officer as required in terms of management policy on processing journals.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Rising borrowing costs present a material risk to the council's financial sustainability.
findings.detail: EY identified as a value-for-money risk that the current level of external debt and the impact of increased borrowing costs pose a significant risk to the Council's financial sustainability. The council has replaced short-term with long-term borrowing to reduce interest rate volatility, but the underlying scale of debt servicing costs remains a material concern.
findings.matters: Higher debt servicing costs consume growing portions of the budget, reducing flexibility to respond to demand shocks, service changes, or other financial pressures. Combined with reserve depletion, this creates a structural funding crisis.
findings.figures: £40 million asset disposal programme undertaken to achieve interest and cost reduction savings
findings.quote: Risk 1 – Level of external borrowing - The current level of debt and the impact of increased borrowing costs presents a risk to the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Council's Stability and Resilience Reserve will be fully depleted by 2027/28 if savings targets are not met.
findings.detail: EY identified a VFM risk of significant weakness: the Council is using its Stability and Resilience Reserve to balance the budget in the short term, and the reserve will be drawn down entirely over the MTFS period if projected savings do not materialise. This would leave the Council with insufficient reserves to set a balanced budget or absorb any further deficit in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion within 2-3 years creates immediate liquidity crisis risk. Without adequate reserves, the council cannot manage spending volatility or implement emergency measures, forcing service cuts or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Reserves projected to be exhausted by 2027/28 if current trajectory continues
findings.quote: The Stability and Resilience Reserve is being used to balance the budget in the short-term and will be depleted over the MTFS period, if no savings materialise. Therefore, the Council will have insufficient reserves in 2027/28 to set a balanced budget or cover further projected deficit.

findings.paper_title: Rushmoor Borough Council - 2024.25 - EY Draft Audit Results Report
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion anticipated for 2024/25 because sufficient evidence cannot be obtained over financial statement balances.
findings.detail: EY anticipates issuing a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements. Although the level of assurance gained has increased, the auditor has not obtained sufficient evidence over all in-year movements and closing balances. Because the 2023/24 audit was also disclaimed, there is no assurance over brought-forward balances from that year. The auditor is unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means no reliance can be placed on the council's published financial statements. This is a fundamental red flag for lenders and signals severe weaknesses in financial reporting and internal control.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions issued on 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23; 2024/25 anticipated to be disclaimed
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.

news_drafts.headline: Service savings strategy abandoned; discovered significant savings could not be achieved without adversely affecting service delivery
news_drafts.lead: The council has abandoned sustainable cost-cutting and is instead treating short-term reserve depletion as its financial strategy, suggesting structural problems with its cost base.

news_drafts.headline: Council reserves will be drawn down to fund structural deficits, with estimated £2.253m available at Vesting Day before risks
news_drafts.lead: The council is structurally deficit and treating reserves as a funding source, not a contingency, with limited buffer remaining against the material risks identified.
